title: Pauri 32, meaning: the steps of the ladder
hook: if one tongue became a hundred thousand, I would repeat the Name on each; these are the steps to the Lord (Japji 32)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sound of Pauri 32. Your line was ik doo jeebhau, from one tongue. Did you choose one good thing to say with it? Today, what all those tongues would do, and the end of a week. Day two hundred seventeen.

Look back at the week. Bhugat giaan: wisdom is the meal, and compassion serves the food. Ekaa maaee: one mother, three powers, and the One who sees them, seen though unseen. The storehouses, filled once, for all. That was the end of Nanak's answer to the yogis. Then yesterday, a single tongue multiplied into two million. Then a staircase. A stadium, an old tower, a subway exit when the escalator's broken. Nobody takes it in one leap. You look at the next step, and the next, and somewhere in the middle you stop counting. Today, Pauri 32 shows us a staircase.
screen: `A WEEK: THE MEAL, THE MOTHER, THE STORES.` → `A LONG STAIRCASE.` → `THE NEXT STEP, AND THE NEXT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: from one tongue, a hundred thousand, then two million. Here's what they'd do. Lakh lakh gerraa aakheeah, ek naam jagdees. With each tongue, round after round, a hundred thousand times, I would say the one Name of the Lord of the world. Gerraa is a round, a turn, like one turn of a wheel. Then: et raah pat pavarreeaa, charreeai hoe ikees. On this path are the steps to the Beloved; climbing them, one becomes one with Him. Pavarreeaa, steps. Listen closely and you can hear pauri in it, the name every stanza of Japji carries. A pauri is a stair, a rung of a ladder. The Japji is built out of steps. But Nanak doesn't let the climb go to anyone's head. The next line: sun galaa aakaas kee, keettaa aaee rees. Hearing talk of the heavens, even worms want to copy it. It's a sharp picture of borrowed spiritual talk: people who speak of the top without taking the stairs. And the last line turns everything: Nanak nadaree paaeeai, koorree koorrai tthees. By grace it is reached; the boasting of the false is false. So there are two halves, and Sikh teachers hold them together. The repeating, round after round, is real effort, a real staircase. And the arrival is a gift, the glance of grace. You climb, step by step. You don't brag about the top.
screen: `A NAME REPEATED, ROUND AFTER ROUND.` · `PAVARREEAA — THE STEPS, LIKE PAURI.` · `EVEN WORMS COPY TALK OF HEAVEN.` · `CLIMB, BUT GRACE BRINGS YOU THERE.` · then, large: `STEP BY STEP.`

segments.voice: In simran, Sikhs repeat Waheguru, a name for the Wondrous Lord. If you'd like, say it twenty times, softly, counting each one on a finger, one step each: Waheguru. Let it be slow; there's no race to the top. If that word isn't yours, count twenty slow breaths instead, each one a step. When you reach twenty, stop climbing. Just stand on that step and rest, breathing. The bell holds the time.
Pauri 32. One Name repeated on a million tongues: these are the steps to the Beloved. The word for steps echoes pauri itself, and arriving is by grace.
Your line: step by step. Today, take one thing you've been dreading and do only the first step of it. Just the first. Day two hundred seventeen.

howItsDone: Sikhs repeat Waheguru in simran, sometimes counting on the fingers or on a mala; Pauri 32 pictures repetition of the Name as a staircase, with the arrival given by grace.

original.note: Gurmukhi, Japji Pauri 32: the steps; it echoes pauri, a stair or rung.

trapdoor: what you thought: a ladder to heaven.
what it means: repeating the Name, round after round, is the stair toward the Beloved, and grace is what lets you arrive.
what a scholar hears: pavarreeaa echoes pauri, the name of the stanza form itself; hoe ikees is read as becoming one with the Lord.

Gurmukhi quoted in transliteration as the original; English is paraphrase. Macauliffe 1909 not quoted because not verified word for word.
pavarreeaa and pauri (stair, ladder) presented as the same word family; confirm.
hoe ikees read as becoming one with the Lord (ik + ees); some commentators also note ikees as the number twenty-one. Left out of the voice; confirm.
